question: Synthesize what the corpus says about self-repair in code generation: describe the repair workflow, explain how LiveCodeBench evaluates related capabilities, and explain why counterfeit-samples work recommends caution with self-repair or model-based reranking.
answer:
The corpus describes self-repair as a multi-step pipeline: a program is first sampled from a code generation model, then executed against unit tests, and if it fails, the error message and faulty program are sent to a feedback generation model that produces a short explanation of what is wrong; that explanation is then passed to a repair model, which generates a fixed version of the program [Source 3]. The paper also notes that this is attractive because it can correct unlucky decoding samples and incorporate symbolic feedback, but it costs extra model invocations, so the key question is whether self-repair beats simply sampling more programs under the same compute budget [Source 3].

On evaluation of related capabilities, the corpus says that self-repair is not just “code generation” in disguise: prior work argues that code understanding is an integral part of the repair pipeline, because success depends on the model’s ability to generate accurate textual explanations of what is wrong with the code [Source 1]. So self-repair is used as a probe of whether the model can understand faulty code well enough to diagnose and then fix it [Source 1].

For why the counterfeit-samples work recommends caution with self-repair or model-based reranking, the key point is that counterfeit samples behave adversarially to the model. The paper reports that models often struggle to assess their correctness, reason about their execution as if they were correct programs, and repair them at a low rate [Source 2]. It also finds an inconsistency between generation and understanding: even counterfeit samples from problems that are easier for the model to solve are only slightly easier to assess, execute, and repair [Source 2]. Because “understanding counterfeit samples is a prerequisite to many downstream applications in which models use their own feedback to improve themselves,” the authors recommend exercising caution with schemes such as self-repair and model-based reranking of outputs [Source 2].

In short: self-repair is a generate–test–explain–fix workflow [Source 3]; it evaluates a model’s code understanding as much as its generation ability [Source 1]; and counterfeit samples suggest caution because models may be poor at judging and repairing their own outputs, making self-improvement schemes unreliable [Source 2].

typical workflow. First, a program is sampled from a code generation model; this program is then run
on a suite of unit tests provided as part of the specification; if the program fails any test, then the error
message and the faulty program are given to a feedback generation model, which outputs a short
explanation of why the code failed; finally, the feedback is passed to a repair model, which generates
a fixed version of the program.1 On the surface, this is a very attractive idea. It allows the system to
overcome mistakes caused by unfortunate samples during decoding; easily incorporates feedback
during the repair phase from symbolic systems such as compilers, static analysis tools, and execution
engines; and mimics the trial-and-error way in which human software engineers write code.
However, it is important to remember that self-repair requires more invocations of the model, thus
increasing the computational cost. In particular, whether self-repair is a winning strategy or not
ultimately boils down to whether you would—at an equivalent compute budget—have had a greater
chance of success if you had simply drawn more code samples i.i.d. from the model and checked them
